true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook secret compared non-constant-time; no method check; parse errors give 500s

- The shared secret is compared with `!==`, which is not timing-safe; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.
- The handler accepts any HTTP method.
- `schema.parse` throws on a bad body, and `symmetricDecrypt` / `JSON.parse` throw on a bad payload or wrong key. These surface as unhandled 500s instead of 400s.

false_positives.candidate:
Inconsistent app slug sent to sync endpoint

Zoom sends `appSlug: "zoomvideo"`, but the app's slug is `zoom`, which is what the credential uses as `appId` and what the webhook expects. A self-hosted sync endpoint keyed by slug will not recognise the Zoom request.

Outbound token-sync request carries no authentication

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`, with no secret, signature or header. The self-hoster's endpoint cannot verify that the caller is Cal.com, yet it is expected to return live OAuth access tokens for arbitrary user ids. The request should include the webhook secret header or an equivalent signature.

`prisma` used without being imported

`prisma.credential.update` is called, but `@calcom/prisma` is never imported in this file. This is a compile error, or at runtime a ReferenceError that rejects `getClient`, so every Salesforce operation fails.

appStoreMetadata looked up by slug instead of directory name

`appStoreMetadata` is keyed by app directory name, e.g. `googlecalendar`, `office365calendar`, `zoomvideo`. The handler indexes it with the DB slug, e.g. `google-calendar`, `zoom`. For most apps the lookup returns undefined and the webhook responds 404 "App not found". Look up by matching `slug` across the values instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive

The blacklist entries are lowercased, but each `guest` is compared as-is. A blacklisted address written with any uppercase letter (e.g. `Bad@x.com`) passes the filter. The attendee check `guest === attendee.email` is also case-sensitive, so an existing attendee can be added again as a duplicate by changing the casing. Normalize guest emails to lowercase before both comparisons.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, so it is only true when both checks pass. The name and intent call for OR. Depending on how `isTeamAdmin` is implemented, plain team admins are denied permission they are meant to have.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Emails use raw `guests` instead of the filtered `uniqueGuests`

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` receives the original input list, not `uniqueGuests`. If the input includes someone who is already an attendee, that person is treated as a brand-new guest and gets a fresh `AttendeeScheduledEmail` instead of the 'guests added' update. The intended split between new and existing attendees is therefore wrong whenever the input overlaps the current attendee list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email-disable settings

Every other booking email sender checks `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` and `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail` against the event type metadata. `sendAddGuestsEmails` accepts no metadata and always emails organizers, team members and attendees. This sends mail even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add unlimited arbitrary emails, enabling spam

Any attendee of a booking may call this endpoint. The schema puts no limit on the number of guests, and the handler does not check booking status (cancelled, past, etc.). Each call sends emails from the platform to arbitrary addresses, so the endpoint can be abused to send spam. Add a maximum list size and a status check, and reconsider whether attendees should have this permission.

Calendar update failure after DB write leaves inconsistent state

Attendees are inserted with `prisma.booking.update` before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` runs, and that call is not wrapped in error handling. If the calendar update throws, the client sees an error, yet the guests are already saved and no emails are sent. A retry then fails with `emails_must_be_unique_valid` because the guests now exist. Wrap the call in error handling or order the operations so the result stays consistent.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

The `EventManager` is built from `ctx.user` and that user's credentials. When a team admin or an attendee (both allowed by the permission check) adds guests, the booking's calendar and video references belong to the organizer. `updateCalendarAttendees` will either fail or touch the wrong account. The organizer's credentials (`booking.user.credentials`) should be used instead.

Error fallback message is unreachable

`message` is a template string such as `"undefined: ..."`, which is always truthy. As a result, `t("unable_to_add_guests")` is never shown, and users can see text like 'undefined: ...'.

Validation error is never cleared after a successful submit

`isInvalidEmail` is set to true on a failed validation. It is only reset by the Cancel button, not when the input is corrected, when a submit succeeds, or when the dialog is closed via `onOpenChange`. A stale 'Emails must be unique and valid' warning therefore stays visible after the problem is fixed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry-count delete branch is not restricted to SMS reminders

The second `OR` branch of `deleteMany` is `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter. This SMS cron will delete any `WorkflowReminder` whose `retryCount` exceeds 1, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders. Today only this handler increments the column, but the column is generic on the model. As soon as another scheduler uses `retryCount`, this job will silently wipe that scheduler's reminders. Move the method filter outside the `OR`, or add it to the retry branch.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
OR on unindexed retryCount likely forces a full table scan each cron run

Adding `OR retryCount > 1` with no method filter means Postgres cannot use only the existing `(method, scheduled, scheduledDate)` index. With no index on `retryCount`, this `deleteMany` will probably scan the entire `WorkflowReminder` table on every cron invocation. The cost grows with the table, which holds email and WhatsApp reminders as well as SMS ones.

Reminders with no message or recipient are never counted as retries

When `message` is empty or `sendTo` is null (e.g. missing `smsReminderNumber`), neither branch of the new retry logic runs. These permanently unschedulable reminders are re-fetched and reprocessed on every cron run until their scheduled date passes, which is the behaviour this PR is meant to stop. Increment `retryCount`, or delete the reminder, in this case too.

Unguarded DB update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The `catch` block now awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update` before logging. If this update fails (DB error, or the reminder was deleted concurrently, e.g. booking cancelled), the error escapes the `for` loop. The request returns a 500 and all remaining reminders in the batch are skipped. The original error is also never logged because the `console.log` comes after the update. Wrap the update in its own try/catch, or log first and swallow the update error.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead branches in getBaseConditions

`authConditions` is always a `Prisma.Sql` object and therefore always truthy, including NOTHING_CONDITION. The `else if (filterConditions)` and final `else` branches can never run. This misleadingly suggests the filter-only path could skip authorization. Simplify to: return auth alone when there is no filter, otherwise return auth AND filter.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Authorization fragments are top-level ORs without outer parentheses

For org and team scope, `getAuthorizationConditions()` returns `(A) OR (B)` with no wrapping parentheses. A single eventTypeId filter likewise returns `(x) OR (y)` unwrapped. `getBaseConditions()` adds parentheses, but both getters are public. A consumer that writes `WHERE ${auth} AND "createdAt" > ...` or `WHERE ${filter} AND ${auth}` gets `A OR (B AND ...)` because of SQL operator precedence. That silently widens results and can bypass the authorization restriction. Return self-contained, parenthesized fragments, e.g. ``Prisma.sql`((${acc}) OR (${condition}))` ``.

Caching tests removed and authorization not verified end-to-end

The caching tests for `getAuthorizationConditions` and `getFilterConditions` were deleted rather than ported, so the caching behavior is now untested. The only test that runs SQL against the database uses user scope. The org and team scope fragments, which use `ANY()` array parameters and OR composition, are only compared structurally and never executed. Type or precedence errors in those fragments would therefore go unnoticed.

Constructor type weakened so invalid options compile and silently yield no data

The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId` is optional for every scope. Passing `scope: "team"` without `teamId` now type-checks. It then fails zod validation at runtime and silently becomes NOTHING_CONDITION (empty results) instead of being a compile-time error. The discriminated union type would catch this at compile time.

Public findMany() removed and replaced by getBaseConditions(), breaking existing callers

The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method is deleted. In its place is `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment instead of rows. Any caller that does `service.findMany({ select, where, ... })` (for example the insights routers) will no longer compile. Those call sites would also need rewriting to use `$queryRaw`, and the PR does not update any of them. Either keep a compatibility path or update every consumer in the same PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plain Error instead of TRPCError for not-found/forbidden

Throwing a generic `Error` when the credential doesn't belong to the user makes tRPC return an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500). It also gets logged as a server fault. Use `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" | "FORBIDDEN" })` so clients get a proper 4xx response and logs aren't polluted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timestamp formatted with hardcoded en-US locale

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` ignores the user's locale even though the surrounding string is translated. Non-US users will see US-style dates (MM/DD/YY, 12h clock) inside localized text. Use the locale from `useLocale()` (i18n.language) instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status includes expired entries

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups over all CalendarCache rows regardless of `expiresAt`. `getCachedAvailability` only serves rows with `expiresAt >= now`. The UI can therefore show a cache as present and "last updated" when every entry is expired and nothing would actually be served from cache. Filter on `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`.

Cache status stays stale after a successful cache delete

The `deleteCache` mutation's `onSuccess` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop. It never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, unlike the disconnect mutation, which does so in `onSettled`. `onChanged` is often undefined, and the query uses `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`. As a result, after deleting the cache the dropdown keeps showing "Cache Status / Last updated" and the delete option until a full reload, so it looks like the delete did nothing.

Extra no-op updateMany on every cache refresh

`updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` runs on every `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`, which fires on each Google webhook. With empty `data`, whether Prisma bumps `updatedAt` at all is unreliable. Per the PR notes, `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not consumed anywhere; the UI reads `CalendarCache.updatedAt`. This adds a write across all selected calendars of the credential on a hot path for no functional benefit and should be removed.

Migration warning contradicts the SQL; legacy rows get misleading timestamp

The header warns that the column is added "without a default value", but the statement does use `DEFAULT NOW()`. That stale autogenerated comment should be removed. Also, every existing cache row gets the migration time as `updatedAt`, so the UI will report legacy caches as freshly updated at deploy time.

No tests for new handler or repository method

There are no unit tests for `deleteCacheHandler`, including its ownership check and the case of a credential belonging to another user. There are also none for `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` or for the cache enrichment in `connectedCalendarsHandler`. The PR itself notes it was never tested end-to-end.

UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt/googleChannelId

`getConnectedDestinationCalendars` is re-exported for `@calcom/platform-libraries`. Widening the required Pick fields on the input type forces every external caller (e.g. API v2) to select `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` on selected calendars. Otherwise their type check breaks, yet these fields are never used by this function.

dev:cron depends on undeclared tsx via npx

`npx tsx` relies on `tsx`, which is not declared in dependencies. npx will download it on demand, which can prompt or fail in offline or CI environments and leaves the version unpinned. `ts-node` is still in devDependencies. Either add `tsx` as a devDependency or keep `ts-node`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation calls are fire-and-forget

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async but are called inside `forEach` without being awaited. The handler can return before the `cancelled` flag update or the Twilio cancel and DB delete finish.

In serverless deployments, work still pending after the response may be dropped. A dropped flag update means the cron never cancels the email. Previously the DB deletes were at least awaited through `Promise.all`, and the same regression applies in bookings.tsx `requestReschedule` and in workflows.tsx.

Fix: collect the promises and await them.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete branch never removes the DB record

When `immediateDelete` is true, the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns. It never deletes or flags the WorkflowReminder row.

For workflow or step deletion, the row is removed later by cascade. Other callers, such as the reschedule path in handleNewBooking, are left with a row that still says `scheduled: true` and has no `cancelled` flag. That row is inconsistent with reality and is only cleaned up after its scheduledDate passes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Deferred cancellation can miss reminders that are close to their send time

Cancellation only marks `cancelled: true`. The real SendGrid cancel waits for the next cron run, which happens every 15 minutes.

Suppose a booking is cancelled or rescheduled shortly before a reminder's send time, for example right after a cron tick and less than about 15–25 minutes before sendAt. The next cron run may come too late, either after the send or inside SendGrid's minimum lead time for cancelling a scheduled send. The email for the cancelled booking is still delivered, which is the bug this PR is meant to fix.

Fix: cancel immediately when scheduledDate is within the cron window (for example under 1h15m away), and defer only reminders further in the future.

One failed SendGrid cancel aborts all remaining cancellations in the cron run

The loop awaits `client.request` for each cancelled reminder inside a single try/catch. If one request throws (invalid batch id, rate limit, or the 100 pending-cancellation cap), the loop stops. Every remaining reminder in that run is left uncancelled.

The delete operations already collected are lazy Prisma promises that only run at `Promise.all`, which is never reached. So even reminders that were cancelled successfully stay in the DB. The failing reminder is likely to break subsequent runs the same way until its scheduledDate passes, and the affected emails go out.

Fix: wrap each reminder in its own try/catch and delete each row right after its cancel succeeds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach callback escapes the surrounding try/catch

The callback was changed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })`. Any error from `getCalendar` (for example a CalendarService constructor throwing on a bad credential key) is now a rejected promise. The enclosing `try/catch` never sees it, so it becomes an unhandled rejection.

Before this change `getCalendar` was synchronous, so a throw was caught and logged. The deletions are also fire-and-forget, so the function returns before they complete.

Fix: use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dynamic imports run eagerly at module load, so nothing is lazy-loaded

Each entry is written as `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`. That calls `import()` immediately when `@calcom/app-store` is first evaluated, so all ~28 app packages still load up front, just asynchronously. The PR's goal (only loading an app when it is used) is not achieved. Meanwhile every consumer had to become async, which adds the problems listed in the other findings.

There is a second risk: if any single app module fails to import, its promise rejects at load time with no handler attached. That produces an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process depending on configuration.

Fix: use thunks such as `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` and have callers invoke the thunk.

false_positives.candidate:
Async forEach callback escapes the surrounding try/catch

This has the same problem as the vital reschedule. The `forEach(async ...)` callback awaits `getCalendar`, so a failure while loading or constructing the calendar becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The surrounding try/catch cannot catch it, although it could catch the previously synchronous throw.

Fix: use `await Promise.all(...map(async ...))` inside the try block.

Dynamic imports run eagerly at module load, so nothing is lazy-loaded

Each entry is written as `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`. That calls `import()` immediately when `@calcom/app-store` is first evaluated, so all ~28 app packages still load up front, just asynchronously. The PR's goal (only loading an app when it is used) is not achieved. Meanwhile every consumer had to become async, which adds the problems listed in the other findings.

There is a second risk: if any single app module fails to import, its promise rejects at load time with no handler attached. That produces an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process depending on configuration.

Fix: use thunks such as `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` and have callers invoke the thunk.

Recurring-cancel deletes are pushed into apiDeletes after it is awaited

In the recurring branch, `forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(...) })` pushes into `apiDeletes` only after an await. By that point `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 has already captured the array.

As a result, these calendar deletions are never awaited, and any errors they throw are unhandled rejections. The new `await getCalendar` makes this race certain rather than incidental.

Fix: use a `for...of` loop like the non-recurring branch below.

getCalendarCredentials now returns `calendar` as a Promise, silently changing its contract

`getCalendarCredentials` still calls `getCalendar(credential)` without awaiting it. The `calendar` field of each returned item is therefore now `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`.

Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`. Any other caller that uses `item.calendar` directly will now operate on a Promise. That includes truthiness checks like `if (!calendar)`, which are always truthy for a Promise, and calls like `calendar.listCalendars()`.

Also, a rejection of a promise created here before `getConnectedCalendars` attaches a handler can surface as an unhandled rejection.

requestReschedule fires un-awaited async callbacks; getCalendar failures become unhandled rejections

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` is not awaited. If `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` rejects, nothing handles the rejection, and it can crash or log noise in the API process.

The mutation also returns before the old calendar and video events are deleted. Previously a synchronous `getCalendar` throw would have surfaced as a proper TRPC error.

Fix: use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` with error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check uses the slot start time as its end time

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, exactly like `start`. The check therefore never compares the slot's real end (`slotEndTime`) against `workingHour.endTime`. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end is treated as available, so meetings can be booked that overrun a fixed host's working hours.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with `===` (always false)

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two distinct object references, so the condition is never true. Zero-length overrides, which mark the user unavailable all day, are not handled by this branch. A slot that straddles the zero-length point then passes the later checks. Use `.isSame()` here.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple date-override ranges on one day reject slots inside later ranges

`dateOverrides.find` returns true, meaning 'not available', for the first same-day override whose range does not contain the slot. If a user has two override ranges on the same day (e.g. 9-10 and 14-16), a slot at 14:00 is rejected because it falls outside 9-10, even though it fits the second range. The slot should be accepted if any override range for that day contains it.

Offset-shifted override can wrap past midnight and produce an invalid range

Start and end are computed as hour*60+minute after adding the timezone offset. When the shift crosses midnight (e.g. an override ending 22:00 shifted by +3h becomes 01:00), `endTime` ends up smaller than `startTime`. `buildSlots` skips such ranges (`start >= end`), so the override silently yields no slots. Meanwhile it has still removed the user's working hours for that day. The `activeOverrides` filter also uses the unshifted UTC start, so it can choose the wrong invitee day.

Override day matching mixes shifted organizer time with UTC slot date

The override start is shifted by the negated organizer offset and formatted as a date. That date is then compared with the slot's UTC calendar date (`slotStartTime` is `.utc()`). For organizers far from UTC, the organizer's local override day and the slot's UTC day differ near midnight. As a result, overrides can be ignored for slots on the override day, or applied to slots on an adjacent day.

Override end boundary compares slot start instead of slot end

The slot is rejected only when `slotStartTime` is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override ends but runs past it (e.g. a 60-minute slot at 10:30 with an override ending at 11:00) passes the check. The fixed host is then booked outside their overridden availability. The check should compare `slotEndTime` against the override end.

Parsing Date.toString() output with dayjs is non-standard

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` parses the locale-style `Date.prototype.toString()` string, which is not ISO 8601. That depends on engine-specific `Date` parsing and drops milliseconds. `override.start` is already a `Date` and should be passed directly.

Round-robin fixed-host override fix is not tested

The PR's main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides restrict round-robin availability, but no test creates a round-robin event with a fixed host that has an override. The added test only covers a personal event in a second timezone. The existing `toHaveTimeSlots` matcher also does not check the slot count, so missing expected slots go undetected. None of the new `checkIfIsAvailable` paths are covered: multiple ranges, slots running past the override end, and zero-length overrides.

Split working hours reject valid slots

`workingHours.find` returns true as soon as any working-hour entry for that weekday does not contain the slot, and that makes the slot unavailable. If a host has several ranges on the same day (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17, or ranges split at the UTC day boundary), a slot inside 9-12 lies outside 13-17 and gets rejected. The fix is to reject only when the slot falls outside all applicable ranges (use `some`/`every` correctly). As written, fixed and round-robin hosts with multiple ranges lose valid slots.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when integration metadata has no `sender`

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every existing Integration has a `sender` entry. `build_integration` only sets it when `state.get("sender")` is present, and older integrations or ones created through other paths may not have it. In those cases this line raises an uncaught KeyError, and the user gets a 500 instead of the error page. Use `.get()` and treat a missing sender as a failed check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user check is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet

When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist`, the view returns `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anyone. That happens whenever the installation webhook has not arrived or been processed yet. `build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app JWT and creates the integration for whatever `installation_id` was supplied in the query string. Someone who knows another account's installation_id can win this race and bind that GitHub installation to their own Sentry org, which is the attack this PR is meant to stop. The installer identity should be checked in this branch too, for example by comparing against the installation's sender or account from the GitHub API, or the step should fail closed.

OAuth authorize URL is built without URL-encoding parameters

`redirect_uri` is an absolute URL containing `:` and `/` characters, and `client_id` and `state` are interpolated raw into the query string. If the configured URL prefix ever contains `?`, `&`, `#` or similar characters, the query string to GitHub will be malformed. Build it with `urlencode({...})`.

Unhandled exceptions in the OAuth token exchange and user lookup

`safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 is outside the try block, so network or connection errors propagate. The HTTP status of the response is never checked. `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` raises an API error when GitHub returns a non-2xx response, for example a revoked token or rate limiting. All of these escape `dispatch` as a 500 instead of rendering the 'Invalid installation request' error page that the PR says users will see in these cases.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests a missing installation

The test now sends a `state` (`ddd023...`) that does not match the pipeline signature. It therefore fails at the state check in OAuthLoginView and never reaches `build_integration`. The 404 branch ('The GitHub installation could not be found.') is no longer covered. Use the correct state value and restore the original assertion. Add a separate test for the state-mismatch case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain default value, so Python evaluates it once when the class is defined. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` (including every one from `from_integration`) gets the timestamp of process startup, not of the assignment. Any later use of `queued` for ordering, staleness or debouncing would be wrong. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Raw datetime placed in Celery task kwargs; deserialized type is not validated

`assignment_source.to_dict()` uses `dataclasses.asdict`, which leaves `queued` as a `datetime` object, and that dict is passed as a Celery task kwarg. With a JSON task serializer this either fails to serialize or arrives on the worker as a string. `AssignmentSource.from_dict` then does `cls(**input_dict)` with no type conversion, so `queued` silently becomes a `str` despite being typed as `datetime`. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. ISO string or epoch) in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
New `assignment_source` kwarg passed to every integration's `sync_assignee_outbound`

The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)` on every provider. Any concrete implementation (Jira, Jira Server, VSTS, GitHub, example, etc.) whose override lacks `**kwargs` will raise `TypeError`, and outbound assignee sync will break for that provider. Confirm that all overrides accept the kwarg, or add it to their signatures.

New task kwarg is not safe during a rolling deploy

Producers now always send `assignment_source_dict` to `sync_assignee_outbound` (even when its value is None). During a rolling deploy, workers still running the old task signature will receive the unexpected kwarg and raise `TypeError`, so assignee syncs fail until every worker is updated. The usual pattern is to deploy the task parameter first and start sending it in a follow-up change.

No end-to-end test that inbound sync suppresses outbound to the same integration

The new test calls `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` directly with an `AssignmentSource`. Nothing exercises `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (assign or deassign) to check that it no longer triggers `sync_assignee_outbound` for the originating integration, which is the cycle this PR is meant to break. There is also no `to_dict`/`from_dict` round-trip test through the task, which would have exposed the datetime serialization problem.

`sync_status_outbound` gains `assignment_source` but nothing passes it

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature now accepts `assignment_source`, but no caller provides it and status sync does not go through `should_sync` with a source. The same inbound-to-outbound cycle for status changes is therefore not prevented, while the signature implies it is. Either wire the source through the status sync path or drop the unused parameter.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. That leaves several abstract members unimplemented: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.

As a result, `process_detectors` crashes for these detectors instead of returning no results, which is what the previous stub did.

Fix: either implement the methods (stubbed for now) or keep the old non-stateful stub until the real implementation lands.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

The `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". The method now returns a dict keyed by `DetectorGroupKey`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

Mock occurrence ignores value and uses identical ids, so tests can't catch wrong-value or cross-group mixups

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores its `value` argument, and every occurrence uses the same hard-coded `id` and `event_id`. Expected occurrence built for wrong group key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe

Moved/renamed helpers removed from mark_failed with no compatibility re-exports

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' here vs 'shard' elsewhere

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `shards`, while `flusher.produce`, `segment_size_bytes` and `flusher_unhealthy` use `shard`. Dashboards and queries that filter or group by `shard` will miss this metric. In addition, the tag value is a comma-joined list of shards (e.g. "0,4,8") on some metrics and a single shard elsewhere, which adds tag cardinality and makes the values inconsistent.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process", does nothing. The test still relies on the flusher thread happening to flush before it sees `stopped` in `join()`. It therefore stays timing-dependent and potentially flaky, despite the comment suggesting otherwise.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhealthy flusher processes are never killed because the isinstance check misses SpawnProcess

Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, so each one is a `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process`, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False in production. The old code called `kill()` unconditionally; with the new guard, a hung flusher is never killed. A replacement process is still spawned for the same shards, so two processes flush the same shards at once. That can produce duplicate or fragmented segments, and leaked processes pile up with each restart. Check for `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` instead, or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`. The same wrong check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process", does nothing. The test still relies on the flusher thread happening to flush before it sees `stopped` in `join()`. It therefore stays timing-dependent and potentially flaky, despite the comment suggesting otherwise.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() stops early and skips terminating the remaining processes once the deadline passes

When the deadline is exceeded, the loop does `break`. Every process after that point is left without `terminate()` being called. This happens often, because `next_step.join(timeout)` runs first and can use up most of the timeout. Those flusher processes keep running past consumer shutdown or rebalance and may still touch Redis and Kafka for shards that are no longer assigned. The loop should skip the waiting but still terminate every remaining process.

false_positives.candidate:
Docstring claims one process per shard, but the CLI default is a single process

The class docstring says it "Creates one process per shard". The `--flusher-processes` CLI option defaults to 1, so in production all shards share a single process unless the option is set explicitly. One process per shard only happens when `max_processes` is None or 0.

Restart limit is now counted per process, so total allowed restarts scales with process count

`MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` used to cap the total number of flusher restarts before the consumer is failed. It is now tracked separately for each process index. With N processes, the consumer tolerates up to N*(MAX+1) crashes before raising, which weakens the crash-loop safeguard.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `Commit`, roughly once per second. Arroyo's commit callback is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the strategy's `submit`/`poll` on the consumer thread.

Calling it concurrently with the `StreamProcessor` run loop can corrupt its staged-offset state. It can also commit after the processor has started revoking partitions or shutting down, because `terminate()` doesn't join this thread. Collect committable offsets here, but perform the commit inside `poll()` on the main thread.

Commits stall permanently when partition offsets are not contiguous

`get_committable_offsets` only advances while every integer offset between `start` and `max_offset` has been seen in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control records, compacted topics, and aborted transactions all leave gaps that the consumer never receives.

Any such gap blocks commits for that partition forever, while `all_offsets` keeps growing. Track contiguity only among the offsets actually received (for example, commit up to just below the lowest outstanding offset), not across absolute integer ranges.

Error-handling test asserts no commit, contrary to implementation, and passes only by timing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts that the partition is not committed after one processing failure. The implementation does mark failed offsets complete, so both 100 and 101 become committable and are committed on the next one-second commit tick.

The test passes only because it exits roughly 0.2s after processing finishes, before the commit thread wakes up. It is flaky on slow CI, and it documents behavior the code doesn't have. Assert the real semantics deterministically instead.

Failed items are committed, contradicting "only commits after successful processing"

The worker's `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raises. Decode and submit failures are also completed immediately. Offsets are therefore committed regardless of processing outcome, which is at-most-once delivery. The class docstring says "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and "No item is lost", which is misleading for anyone relying on it.

Shared queue pool is shut down on rebalance, so later messages are silently dropped and committed

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `__init__`, but every `create_with_partitions` call wraps that same pool in a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On a partition revocation or rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy. That calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down every queue and stops every worker permanently.

The next strategy built after reassignment reuses the dead pool:
- `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
- `submit` catches it in its generic `except`, then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for that message.
- The commit loop commits those offsets.

After the first rebalance, every uptime result is dropped but its offset is still committed. Either build the pool per strategy, or don't shut down the shared pool in the strategy's `close()`.

Shutdown discards queued work and never commits work that finished after the last tick

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. Each worker exits after its current item, so items still waiting in the queues are never processed. `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)` would normally drain them, but the flag defeats that.

In `close()`, the commit thread is also stopped before the pool shuts down. Offsets for items that finished in the final window are never committed, so they are reprocessed after reassignment.

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and does no draining either. On rebalance this produces both skipped items (in-memory loss, recovered only by redelivery) and duplicates. Drain the queues, wait for workers, then do a final commit before returning from `join`.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure, despite the docstring

Each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A single slow subscription will therefore let its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, risking OOM. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and raise `MessageRejected` when one is full.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every new denied resource now bypasses the permission cache and queries the DB

When cached permissions exist but do not grant access, `Check` falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`. That function no longer consults `permCache`, so it always runs the basic-role, team and permission queries against the DB.

The denial cache only short-circuits repeats of the exact (user, action, name, folder) tuple. A user checked against many distinct resources they cannot access triggers a full permission query per resource, for example when filtering a search result set dashboard by dashboard. Singleflight only dedups concurrent identical calls.

Before this change those checks were served from `permCache`. This can multiply DB load substantially for users with restricted access.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not prove the cache short-circuits

The test claims to "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but it seeds `permCache` with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. A false value is not a grant in `checkPermission`.

The default fake store also returns no permissions. So the request would be denied even if the denial cache were ignored, and the test passes regardless of whether `permDenialCache` works.

The cached value should be `true`, and ideally the test should assert the store was not called.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous denial cache key can deny unrelated resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent with `_` and no escaping. Resource names and folder UIDs may legitimately contain underscores.

For example, (name="a_b", parent="") and (name="a", parent="b") produce the same key. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies access to the other.

The key also shares the `.perm_` prefix with `userPermCacheKey` in the same cache backend, which increases collision risk with differently typed entries. Use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous separator or encoding.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache pins stale denials for 30s, undermining the 'requery on miss' fix

Any denial is cached for `shortCacheTTL` (30s), and the denial cache is checked before anything else.

If a check for a resource happens before its permissions are written, the denial sticks. This can occur during a create flow or right before a share or grant. Every subsequent check for that resource then returns denied for 30s without consulting the DB, even after the permission exists.

This reintroduces the delay the PR is trying to eliminate for newly created dashboards and folders. Nothing invalidates the entry when permissions are granted.

Requery does not refresh the stale folder tree, so newly created folders still deny and the denial gets cached

The DB fallback only refreshes the permission scope map. `checkInheritedPermissions` still uses `buildFolderTree`, which is served from `folderCache` (30s TTL).

Scenario: a dashboard sits in a newly created folder whose ancestor grants access. The new folder is missing from the cached tree, so `Ancestors(req.ParentFolder)` yields nothing and the check is denied. That denial is then written to `permDenialCache`, extending the wrong answer.

This is part of the scenario the PR claims to fix (newly created folders) and it remains broken. On a miss, the folder tree should also be refreshed, or the denial should not be cached when the parent folder is absent from the tree.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing `key` prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in rule list map
