true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item shown but does nothing when only promRule is provided

In the list view, AlertRuleMenu shows 'Silence notifications' based on the promRule abilities. Clicking it only sets `showSilenceDrawer`. The drawer renders only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, and `rule` (the ruler rule) is now undefined in the list view. The button is therefore a silent no-op for users.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause never shown in list view despite prom-based permission checks

`canDelete` and `canPause` now OR in the promRule-based abilities. However, the Delete item still requires `rulerRule` to be present (line 165), and the Pause item requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123). The list view no longer passes `rulerRule`, so users with full permissions lose the Delete and Pause actions there. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts exactly 4 menu items, which locks this regression in.

Export/Pause/Restore restricted to alerting rules for Grafana prom rules

The ruler-based hook gates ModifyExport, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently on `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which is true for any Grafana rule, including recording rules. The new prom-based hook uses `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` instead. As a result, Grafana-managed recording rules can no longer be exported or paused from the list view. The variable name suggests 'Grafana-managed' was intended.

Federated rule group detection removed from legacy ability hook

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities(CombinedRule)` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false`. Federated Mimir rule groups in the existing (V1) list and detail views are no longer treated as immutable. Update, Delete and Pause become supported for them.

Rule view link lost `returnTo` parameter

The removed implementation built the href with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })`. The new component drops `returnTo`, so navigating back from the rule detail page no longer returns users to their filtered or scrolled list position.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Front-loaded interpolation passes ad hoc filters that the backend query path likely applies again

`runSplitQuery` now runs `applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` on every target before splitting. The resulting sub-requests keep `filters` (`{ ...request, targets }`) and are sent through `datasource.runQuery`. That backend `query` path normally calls `applyTemplateVariables` per target again with the request's filters.

As a result, ad hoc filters and variable substitution run twice on the already-interpolated expressions. Depending on how ad hoc filters are merged, this can duplicate filters in the final LogQL. It also re-processes values that were already substituted.

Only `$__auto`/`$step` need to be resolved before splitting. Consider interpolating without `filters`, or stripping `filters`/`scopedVars` from the sub-requests, so the backend path does not apply them again.

Shard splitting interpolates queries again downstream, so ad hoc filters can be added more than once

`runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` on each target. It then passes each sub-request to `runSplitQuery`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again with the same `request.filters` (querySplitting.ts:299). After that, `datasource.runQuery`, which goes through the backend `query` path, normally applies template variables a third time.

The old code used `interpolateVariablesInQueries(targets, scopedVars)` and did not pass `filters`. The new call does pass `request.filters`. Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` appends ad hoc filters to the expression, so running it repeatedly can add the same label matchers or label filters more than once (e.g. `| key="v"` repeated) unless every path is idempotent.

Re-interpolation also means a substituted variable value that itself contains `$name` or `${...}` text gets interpolated a second time.

The test 'Interpolates queries before running' asserts `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times (1 + 4 sub-requests), which bakes in this double interpolation instead of catching it.

Fix: interpolate once at the entry point, for example by letting `runSplitQuery` skip interpolation when called from the shard path or via an option, and drop `filters` from the pre-interpolation if the backend path already applies them.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so log calls through it are lost

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver `f`. `LoggerMiddleware` now always logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. As a result, any test that injects a `TestLogger` and asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`, `Message` or `Ctx` will always see zero calls, because the call was recorded on a throwaway instance. Return `f`, or a logger that shares its recorded state, so the fake keeps recording when used through `FromContext`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks other implementations

`FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` is a new method on the widely used `plugins/log.Logger` interface. Every implementation outside the two updated here must now implement it or fail to compile. That includes other fakes and test loggers in the repo, enterprise code and external consumers. Check all implementers, or use a separate optional interface with a type assertion.

No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the FromContext wiring

The pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID and uname fields used to be added explicitly by `LoggerMiddleware`. They now depend on two things: `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` setting contextual attributes, and `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` picking them up. The traceID field likewise now relies only on the contextual log provider. Nothing tests this path. If the middleware is reordered, or the type assertion in `FromContext` falls back to `d.New()`, the 'Plugin Request Completed' log lines would silently lose these fields. Add a test that checks the contextual attributes are present on the logged request.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic count-then-insert lets concurrent new devices exceed the limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then does the upsert in a separate statement, with no transaction or lock. Several new devices arriving at the same time can all read `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The configured limit is therefore not enforced under concurrency, including across multiple Grafana instances.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero RowsAffected is treated as limit reached even for existing devices

`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. On MySQL, RowsAffected counts only rows actually changed by default. `updated_at` has second precision there, so updating an existing device with the same IP, user agent and second-truncated timestamp reports 0 rows. A legitimate, already-registered device would then be rejected as over the limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device cached before store call, so the device limit only blocks the first request

`tagDeviceUI` writes the device into `localCache` (line 87) before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached. For the next 29 minutes, every request from that device hits the cache and gets `nil` back. `Authenticate` then succeeds, so a device over the limit is rejected once and then let in. The device should only be cached after a successful store call, or the cache entry should be removed on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved from a background goroutine into the synchronous auth path

Before this change, `TagDevice` ran in a goroutine with its own timeout. Now it runs inline in `Authenticate` using the request context. A cache miss now adds a COUNT query plus an upsert to request latency when a limit is set (just the upsert otherwise), and slow DB calls directly block anonymous logins. A cancelled request context will also make tagging fail.

New device_limit setting is undocumented and missing from default config

`[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read in code, but this PR adds no entry to `conf/defaults.ini` or `sample.ini` and no documentation. Users have no way to discover the option or learn that 0 means unlimited.

ProvideAnonDBStore signature change can break the wire dependency graph

`ProvideAnonDBStore` now takes a bare `int64`, and `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` builds the store itself instead of receiving `AnonStore`. If the wire provider sets still list `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and the `AnonStore` binding, wire cannot satisfy the `int64` parameter and code generation or build fails. The wire files are not updated in this PR.

Tests miss key device-limit behaviours

The new test only checks that a second new device is rejected. Nothing checks that an existing device can still be updated once the limit is reached. Nothing covers the service or client path, where caching currently bypasses the limit. None of the bugs above would be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, including full ID lists

Every cleanup batch logs at Error level: `Annotations to clean by time/count`, `cleaned annotations ...`, `Tags to clean`, `cleaned tags` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). Each message includes the full `ids` slice, which can hold up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (tens of thousands), and the `err` value, which is always nil at the fetch log sites. The final batch of every loop logs an empty result at Error too. In production this floods logs with huge false error entries on every cleanup run and can trigger error-based alerting. These look like debugging leftovers and should be removed or moved to Debug level without the ID lists.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The ticker driving all cleanup jobs changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is unrelated to the PR's stated goal and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often, adding database load and more chances for lock contention, which is the problem this PR is trying to reduce. It also no longer fits the 9-minute per-run timeout in `clean()`, which was sized for a 10-minute interval. This looks like a testing leftover and should be reverted.

false_positives.candidate:
Bound-parameter path can exceed placeholder limits on MySQL/Postgres

Only SQLite falls back to inlining the IDs. On MySQL and Postgres, `deleteByIDs` always binds one placeholder per ID. Both databases cap a prepared statement at 65535 parameters. If an operator sets `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` above that limit, every cleanup batch fails, whereas the previous subquery-based statement had no parameter limit. Consider capping or chunking the IDs per statement, or inlining the integer IDs for all dialects.

Quadratic string building for inlined SQLite IDs

The loop at lines 610-612 runs `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` once per ID. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n²) in the number of IDs. With the large batch sizes this branch exists for (e.g. 32767, as in the new test), that means heavy allocation and CPU work on every batch. Use a `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` into a single byte buffer instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches the base logger to the context instead of the enriched one

Delete builds `log` with name, kind and method, but then calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. Downstream code that pulls the logger from the context loses those fields. Every other method uses `log` here.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded as storage metric

The background goroutine runs `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` but records the result with `d.recordStorageDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are attributed to unified storage, which skews both metric series.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success metric uses object name as the kind label

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This produces wrong labels and unbounded label cardinality, since there is one series per object name.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request returns

Each background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The handler returns right after starting the goroutine, and the apiserver then cancels that request context. The legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection calls will therefore often fail with `context canceled` before they finish, so legacy storage silently drifts out of sync. The same pattern is at lines 110, 135 and 163. The parent should be `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` so logger values are kept but cancellation is not.

Duplicated go.work.sum entry

The line `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added again even though it already appears a few lines above. The go.work.sum changes look like unrelated local churn that should not be in this PR.

Legacy update reapplies the raw objInfo instead of the result from unified storage

The old code wrapped the unified-storage result in `updateWrapper` so legacy received exactly the stored object. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `Legacy.Update` asynchronously. `UpdatedObject` is then re-evaluated against legacy's own current object. For patch or apply requests this can produce a different result, and resourceVersion preconditions may fail. It also reuses a request-scoped `objInfo` after the request has completed.

Legacy write failures in background goroutines are never logged

The goroutines only record a duration metric with an error flag. They never log the error from the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection call. The previous code logged legacy failures. Now a failed safety write to legacy storage leaves no diagnostic trace beyond a counter, which makes divergence between the two stores hard to investigate.

Mode 3 integration tests check legacy reads immediately after async writes, so they are racy

`doPlaylistTests` creates, updates and deletes through the k8s API, then immediately checks `/api/playlists` and `getFromBothAPIs` for matching legacy results. In mode 3 the legacy writes happen in a goroutine with no synchronization. These assertions can therefore run before legacy has been updated, making the new mode 3 file and unified test cases flaky.

Request object shared with background goroutine while the handler continues using it

`obj` (and `options`) are handed to a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Create`, while the apiserver keeps processing and serializing the response, which may reference the same object returned by storage. Legacy create implementations may mutate the object, for example by setting metadata. This creates a data race. A deep copy (`obj.DeepCopyObject()`) should be passed to the goroutine.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage errors are therefore reported as legacy errors, and storage error metrics are missing. Update has the same mistake at line 129.

Unit tests never verify the async legacy writes

The mode 3 Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection tests do not wait for the background goroutine and do not assert that the legacy store was called. Goroutines may also outlive the test. Legacy store and storage share one mock, so legacy calls silently match the storage expectations. Bugs in the legacy path, such as the context cancellation issue, go undetected.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes redundant manifest reloads

The fast path reads `entryPointAssetsCache` under RLock and releases it. It then takes the write lock and unconditionally reloads, without checking the cache again.

At startup or after a cache miss, many concurrent requests can all see `nil`. Each one then queues on the write lock and re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` in turn, even though the first goroutine already populated the cache. If the CDN path is enabled, each would also issue an HTTP request.

Add a second check after `Lock()` (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`), or use `sync.Once`/singleflight for the non-dev case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature-flag check is dead code

`enableSqlExpressions` reads `FlagSqlExpressions`, negates it, and then returns `false` on both branches. The flag lookup has no effect, and the function name and structure suggest the toggle still controls the feature when it does not.

This is easy to 'fix' later into `return true` while the backend is only a stub, or to misread during review. If the intent is a hard disable, replace it with an explicit constant (or remove the helper) and add a comment that SQL expressions are disabled for CVE-2024-9264 regardless of the flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing SQL expression tests will now fail against the stub DB

`TablesList` now uses the stub `DB`, whose `RunCommands` always returns "not implemented". `sql.QueryFramesInto` also always errors.

Existing tests in `pkg/expr/sql` and `pkg/expr` (e.g. parser tests expecting table names, and SQL command tests calling `NewSQLCommand`/`Execute`) previously ran against DuckDB. They will now fail unless they are removed or skipped.

The PR changes no test files. Either CI breaks, or those tests should be updated to assert the disabled behaviour, for example that a SQL expression query is rejected.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is inaccurate

The feature is implemented but has been deliberately disabled for security reasons. The message will confuse users who enabled the `sqlExpressions` feature flag.

A message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" would be accurate. Returning a proper `errutil` BadRequest, consistent with the other SQL errors, would also help.

Non-reader code paths report a misleading 'error reading SQL command' instead of 'disabled'

`UnmarshalSQLCommand` is used by the legacy node-building path and does not go through `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. On that path, the SQL query reaches `NewSQLCommand`, where `sql.TablesList` fails with "not implemented".

The user then gets a 400 "error reading SQL command", which suggests their SQL is malformed rather than that the feature is disabled. The 'disabled' check should be applied centrally, e.g. in `NewSQLCommand`, so every entry point returns a clear, consistent error.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No per-key guard against concurrent BuildIndex now that the global lock is removed

`BuildIndex` used to run entirely under `cacheMu`. Now the lock is taken only to store the result. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does a check-then-build (`GetIndex` returns nil, then `build`), so two callers can build the same `NamespacedResource` concurrently. Typical callers are two `Search` requests, or a `Search` request racing the async `handleEvent` watcher. The consequences are:
- Duplicate full ListIterator scans.
- The second cache store silently replaces the first index, so writes made to the losing instance are lost.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted.
- For file-based indexes, `bleve.New` on the same directory fails because the path already exists.

The code needs per-key build deduplication, e.g. singleflight or a per-key mutex, rather than either one global lock or none.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock. Builds can now run concurrently and write to the map under `cacheMu.Lock`, from `handleEvent` or `Search` triggering `getOrCreateIndex`. A concurrent map read/write is a data race and can crash with a fatal "concurrent map iteration and map write". Take `cacheMu.RLock()` while iterating.

false_positives.candidate:
Context and lifecycle resources leaked when Init fails in the constructor

If `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns nil without calling `cancel()`. It also does not stop a lifecycle that may already have been initialized, such as the DB backend. The background context and any goroutines started during partial init, like the search watch poller, are leaked. Call `cancel()` (and `lifecycle.Stop` where appropriate) on the error path.

Integration test disabled for postgres without a tracked fix

The storage-server module test is now skipped on postgres, with the note "Works locally". This lands alongside a change that moves DB initialization and index building into server construction, which is exactly what this test exercises. Skipping it removes coverage that could catch startup regressions caused by this PR.

Shared variables mutated from errgroup goroutines in init

Each goroutine in `init` assigns the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization. Both are data races. The PR's goal is to raise indexing concurrency, which makes this more likely to trigger. Use a local `err` inside each goroutine and an atomic counter.

Stop no longer causes requests to be rejected

All per-request `s.Init(ctx)` checks were removed, but `Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". That error used to be returned to callers via `Init` after stop. Now nothing reads it, so requests after `Stop` reach the backend after the watch context is cancelled and the backend's `Stop` has run, instead of failing cleanly. The `initErr` writes in `Stop` are dead code, and the shutdown contract has silently changed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of created IDPs

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` targets an IDP named "alias", not the `idp-alias-N` providers this test creates. The same mistake is repeated at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`.

None of the 21 created IDPs are cleaned up. They leak into the realm for subsequent tests, which can change IDP counts and login-page results in other tests and cause order-dependent failures. Use the actual alias variable in the cleanup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Update skips login-cache invalidation when the org-aware wrapper reports the IDP disabled

`update()` passes `idpById` to `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. `idpById` comes from `getById()`, so it is wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`, and its `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The JPA `getForLogin` query does not look at organization state, so the cached login list can still contain this IDP's id.

Scenario:
1. The organization is disabled.
2. An admin sets `hideOnLogin=true` (or `linkOnly=true`) on one of its IDPs.
3. The original model fails the login predicate because the wrapper says disabled, and the updated model fails it because it is hidden. Both are false, so the method returns early and nothing is invalidated.
4. The organization is re-enabled. Organization updates do not invalidate the login keys.

The stale cached id is then resolved through `getById`. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` only re-checks `isEnabled()`, so the hidden or link-only IDP appears on the login page.

Fix: evaluate the predicate against the stored model without the wrapper (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById`). Alternatively, invalidate whenever any `LoginFilter` field or `BROKER_PUBLIC` changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: ASN1 encoders created and discarded

Lines 114-115 build ASN1Encoder instances for r and s and throw the results away. The same encoding is done again in the return statement. This is leftover code that wastes allocations and should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Any third-party or downstream implementation (custom crypto providers, the separate keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile. Already-compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when `detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order`. Declaring it as a `default` method returning a baseline value would keep compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are now picked silently instead of failing

Detection used to throw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by `order()` and silently takes the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so the sort is stable and ties fall back to ServiceLoader/classpath order. The only notice is a debug log. If a FIPS deployment accidentally ships both the FIPS and default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) providers, it can now quietly run on the non-FIPS provider. The old fail-fast guard should be kept for ties at the highest order, or the FIPS provider should be given a distinct higher order.

Test uses one default-curve key for every algorithm and only checks self round-trip

A single key from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` (JDK default curve: P-256 or P-384 depending on JDK version) is reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The test only asserts that DER→RS→DER→RS gives the same result as the first RS conversion. Because `integerToBytes` truncates or pads, a lossy conversion still passes: on a JDK whose default is P-384, ES256 truncates r/s to 32 bytes and both sides match. The test never checks that a converted DER signature still verifies with `Signature.verify`, never uses the curve that matches each algorithm, and never compares output against the BC-based provider. Encoding bugs would go undetected.

integerToBytes silently truncates values longer than the expected length

When `bytes.length > qLength`, the high-order bytes are dropped without any check. This is correct only when the extra byte is the 0x00 sign byte. For a malformed or mismatched-curve signature where r or s really exceeds `signLength/2` bytes, the method returns a corrupted value instead of throwing an IOException. That produces wrong JWS signatures or misleading verification results. It should reject the value when the dropped bytes are non-zero.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client removal no longer cleans up V2 per-client FGAP resources/permissions

The removal listener is now gated on the V1 `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` feature. Nothing replaces it for V2.

When a client that has a per-client resource in the admin-permissions client is deleted, that resource and its scope permissions stay behind as orphans referencing a non-existent client id. They also keep showing up in permission listings.

If both features were enabled at once, `management()` would return `MgmtPermissionsV2`, whose `clients().setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. That would break client deletion.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the schema resource name instead of client ids and misses per-client resources

`getClientsWithPermission` uses `findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` for each match.

Two problems follow:
- Per-client resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)`, which never sets a type. Only the "Clients" all-resource (created in `init` with `setType`) is ever found.
- When an all-clients permission is granted, the returned set contains the string "Clients" rather than any client id.

Callers that use this set to filter or list clients will either see nothing or get a bogus id. Per-client grants are never reflected.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource` can return null, for example when the schema is not supported for this resource server or the "Clients" resource was never created. Realms initialized before this PR added the Clients type would have no such resource.

The result is passed straight to `findByResource(server, resource)` and then `resource.getScopes()` without a null check. A permission check would then fail with a NullPointerException (500) instead of returning false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc for void require* methods says 'Returns true'

The new Javadoc on `requireView()` (line 96) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 101) says "Returns {@code true} if ...". These methods return void. They should say they throw `ForbiddenException` when the corresponding `can*` check returns false.

getResourceName not extended for Clients resource type

`getResourceName` only maps the Users type to a human-readable name. For the new Clients type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`.

Per-client resources are created without a display name, so the admin API and console will show null or a raw internal UUID instead of the clientId. The all-clients resource will not get a friendly label like "All clients" either.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code 4 is repurposed from 'recreate upgrade' to 'feature disabled'

`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` changes from 4 to 3, and 4 now means `FEATURE_DISABLED`. Any script or automation written against the previous behavior that treats exit code 4 as "recreate required" will now get that meaning for a different condition.

The new value does align with the docs table, but the renumbering should be called out, for example in release or upgrade notes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Appending --features=rolling-updates to the documented command can silently override the user's feature configuration

The `updatecompatibility` macro now appends `--features=rolling-updates` to every documented `update-compatibility` invocation. A CLI `--features` value takes precedence over `KC_FEATURES` or a `features=` entry in keycloak.conf.

A user who already enables other features would copy this command and replace their feature list with only `rolling-updates`. The `metadata` and `check` commands would then capture or compare a configuration that differs from the real deployment. The guide itself warns that omitted configuration leads to incorrect results.

The docs should tell users to add `rolling-updates` to their existing feature list rather than hardcoding the flag.

Docs claim the Operator fails if rolling-updates is not enabled, but this PR adds no such check

The new CAUTION block says that if the `rolling-updates` feature is not enabled, "the {project_name} Operator will fail." No operator code in this PR checks the feature or fails on it.

The example also enables the feature through the Keycloak CR `features` list, which configures the server and not the Operator. The test `UpgradeTest` only enables the feature when a strategy is set.

As written, the statement misleads users about what happens. Either the Operator should validate `spec.update` against the enabled features, or the text should describe the actual behavior.

Feature-disabled path tested only for 'metadata' and without checking the exit code

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only runs the `metadata` subcommand and only asserts the error message. It does not check that the exit code is `FEATURE_DISABLED` (4), which is the documented, scriptable contract. The `check` subcommand's feature-disabled branch is not tested at all.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() is granted to callers who only have VIEW on all groups

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` evaluates `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`. Because any matching scope grants access, an admin with only an all-groups VIEW permission passes `requireManage()`. `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` relies on that check, so a view-only admin can create top-level groups or move existing groups to the top level. This is a privilege escalation. Only `MANAGE` should be accepted here. The interface javadoc for `canManage()` repeats the same error ("VIEW or MANAGE") and should also be corrected.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs instead of group IDs and misses per-group resources

There are three problems in this method.

1. Per-group resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never get a type set. Only the schema's all-groups resource has type "Groups", so `findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` will not return per-group resources.
2. The callback passes `groupResource.getId()` (the authz resource id) into `hasPermission`. That method treats the value as a group id and calls `findByName`, so the lookup always falls back to the all-groups resource.
3. The callback adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result set. Group resources are named by group id, so the set holds resource ids rather than group ids.

Callers use this set as group ids: `UserModel.GROUPS` for user search and `getUsersCount(..., groupIds)`. As a result, user counts for group-scoped admins are wrong, and user search filtering by group either matches nothing or matches incorrectly. The new tests only pass because per-user `canView` filtering is applied afterwards on an unfiltered stream, which also breaks pagination. The method should use `resource.getName()` (the group id) and find per-group resources by a means that does not depend on their type.

false_positives.candidate:
V1 group-removal listener now hits UnsupportedOperationException under V2

Before this change, `MgmtPermissionsV2.groups()` was inherited and returned the V1 `GroupPermissions`. It now returns `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

`AdminPermissions.registerListener` (active when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled) calls `management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)` on every `GroupRemovedEvent`. When V2 is also enabled, `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2`. In that configuration, deleting any group would fail with a 500.

V2 management should either no-op here or the listener should skip V2.

requireManageMembers javadoc references the wrong method

The javadoc for `requireManageMembers` says it throws if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false. The implementations actually check `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`. Readers will be misled about which permission is enforced.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian totpStep1 replaced with Italian text

The Lithuanian `totpStep1` value was replaced with "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:", which is Italian. Lithuanian users of the account theme will see an Italian sentence. It should be a Lithuanian translation, or the key should be removed so it falls back to English.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese bundle gets Traditional Chinese text

The new zh_CN `totpStep1` value "在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：" is written in Traditional Chinese characters (zh_TW style). The rest of the file uses Simplified Chinese, so users will see mixed scripts. It should be something like "在您的手机上安装以下应用之一：".

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
ANCHOR_PATTERN matches any tag starting with 'a'

`</?a[^>]*>` also matches tags such as `<abbr>`, `<address>` or `<area>`, not only `<a ...>`. Those tags would be treated as anchors and compared against the English anchors, producing misleading "Didn't find anchor tag" errors. Require a word boundary, e.g. `</?a(\s[^>]*)?>`.

Anchor mismatch message lacks key and file

The "Didn't find anchor tag ..." message does not say which key or file is affected, unlike the duplicate-key and Illegal HTML messages. When the verifier runs over hundreds of bundles, maintainers cannot locate the offending translation. Include `key` and `file` in the message.

Java MessageFormat syntax introduced into i18next-based bundle

This bundle uses i18next interpolation (`{{0}}`, `{{name}}`), as every other key in the file does. The new `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value uses Java MessageFormat placeholders (`{0}`) and a ChoiceFormat expression (`{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`). i18next will not substitute these, so the account console will show the raw placeholder text to users. Keep the `{{n}}` syntax and use i18next pluralization instead. The same problem applies to the identical change in `js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties`.

Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 replaced with Italian text

`loginTotpStep1` in the Lithuanian login bundle now reads "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:", which is Italian. Lithuanian users will see an Italian instruction on the OTP setup page. Use a Lithuanian string, or drop the key so the English fallback is used.

Missing English bundle throws RuntimeException instead of a reported failure

If the derived English file does not exist, `verifySafeHtml` throws a bare RuntimeException. This happens for files without a locale suffix, or when the path regex derives the wrong name. The exception bypasses the `MojoExecutionException` handling in `verify()`, so the build fails with an unclear stack trace instead of a reported verification error. Throw a `MojoExecutionException`, or report the problem as a message.

No positive test and weakened duplicate-key assertion

Every test only checks that some error is reported. None verifies that a valid bundle, such as an allowed `<b>` in a translation whose English source also contains `<b>`, produces no messages, so false positives would go unnoticed. The duplicate-key assertion was also loosened from `contains` to `hasItem`, so unexpected extra errors for that fixture are no longer caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rawTokenId null check validates grantType instead

The fourth `Objects.requireNonNull` call checks `grantType` again but uses the message "Null rawTokenId not allowed". `rawTokenId` is never validated. A null raw ID is therefore accepted silently, and `encodeTokenId` would produce an ID like `onrtac:null` instead of failing fast. The call should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher uses wrong offset and inverted condition

The grant shortcut occupies characters 4..6 of the prefix (e.g. `ac` in `onrtac`), but the matcher reads `substring(3, 5)`, which is the `ta` in `onrtac`. It also returns false when the substring *equals* the expected shortcut, so the check is inverted. In practice the extracted value almost never equals the shortcut, so the matcher accepts any grant type. The new event assertions in expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken therefore do not verify the encoded grant type at all. The check should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`, ideally with a length check on `items[0]` first.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks custom grant type providers; javadoc contradicts required length

`getShortcut()` is added as an abstract interface method. Every existing third-party `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` implementation will fail to compile, or throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls it. A default implementation would avoid this.

The javadoc also says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", but the decoder requires exactly a 6-character prefix, i.e. a 2-character grant shortcut. A custom grant following the docs would issue tokens whose IDs cannot be decoded: `getTokenContextFromTokenId` throws "Expected length of 6". Shortcut length is not validated anywhere.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Lazy refresh of grant shortcuts skips duplicate validation and can fail token issuance

`postInit` validates that grant shortcuts are unique. The runtime refresh paths in `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` do not. A hot-deployed grant whose shortcut collides with an existing one silently overwrites the `grantsByShortcuts` entry, so existing tokens decode to the wrong grant type.

Separately, any code path that sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` to a value with no registered factory now makes `initToken` throw `IllegalStateException`. Token issuance fails outright instead of degrading to the unknown (`na`) value.

Offline-token flows encode session type as online

The session type comes from `userSession.isOffline()` at the time the access token is created. In `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse` and the ROPC grant, the access token is created before `generateRefreshToken()`. That call creates the offline session, and the online session is then removed when FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS is set or for direct grants.

As a result, the access token issued with an offline token is encoded `on`, while the online session it refers to is deleted. The stated goal of using the session type to look up only one session type (#37662) would then fail to find the session for these tokens.

Public copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context removed

The public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor is removed without replacement. Extensions or custom grant types that wrap or copy the context will break. Removing it is unrelated to the feature. If it is kept, it should also copy the new `grantType` field.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exhausted federated recovery-codes credential is removed from the wrong store

`getCredential(user)` now returns the federated credential first. When `allCodesUsed()` is true, the authenticator still calls `removeStoredCredentialById(id)`, which only works on local (Keycloak DB) credentials. true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

If a FIPS deployment accidentally ships both the FIPS and default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) providers, it can now quietly run on the non-FIPS provider. The old fail-fast guard should be kept for ties at the highest order, or the FIPS provider should be given a distinct higher order.

Test uses one default-curve key for every algorithm and only checks self round-trip

A single key from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` (JDK default curve: P-256 or P-384 depending on JDK version) is reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The test only asserts that DER→RS→DER→RS gives the same result as the first RS conversion. Because `integerToBytes` truncates or pads, a lossy conversion still passes: on a JDK whose default is P-384, ES256 truncates r/s to 32 bytes and both sides match. The test never checks that a converted DER signature still verifies with `Signature.verify`, never uses the curve that matches each algorithm, and never compares output against the BC-based provider. Encoding bugs would go undetected.

integerToBytes silently truncates values longer than the expected length

When `bytes.length > qLength`, the high-order bytes are dropped without any check. This is correct only when the extra byte is the 0x00 sign byte. For a malformed or mismatched-curve signature where r or s really exceeds `signLength/2` bytes, the method returns a corrupted value instead of throwing an IOException. That produces wrong JWS signatures or misleading verification results. It should reject the value when the dropped bytes are non-zero.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Now the lock is taken only to store the result. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does a check-then-build (`GetIndex` returns nil, then `build`), so two callers can build the same `NamespacedResource` concurrently. Typical callers are two `Search` requests, or a `Search` request racing the async `handleEvent` watcher. The consequences are:
- Duplicate full ListIterator scans.
- The second cache store silently replaces the first index, so writes made to the losing instance are lost.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted.
- For file-based indexes, `bleve.New` on the same directory fails because the path already exists.

The code needs per-key build deduplication, e.g. singleflight or a per-key mutex, rather than either one global lock or none.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on rebalance, so later messages are silently dropped and committed

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `__init__`, but every `create_with_partitions` call wraps that same pool in a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On a partition revocation or rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy. That calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down every queue and stops every worker permanently.

The next strategy built after reassignment reuses the dead pool:
- `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
- `submit` catches it in its generic `except`, then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for that message.
- The commit loop commits those offsets.

After the first rebalance, every uptime result is dropped but its offset is still committed. Either build the pool per strategy, or don't shut down the shared pool in the strategy's `close()`.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `Commit`, roughly once per second. Arroyo's commit callback is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the strategy's `submit`/`poll` on the consumer thread.

Calling it concurrently with the `StreamProcessor` run loop can corrupt its staged-offset state. It can also commit after the processor has started revoking partitions or shutting down, because `terminate()` doesn't join this thread. Collect committable offsets here, but perform the commit inside `poll()` on the main thread.

Shutdown discards queued work and never commits work that finished after the last tick

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. Each worker exits after its current item, so items still waiting in the queues are never processed. `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)` would normally drain them, but the flag defeats that.

In `close()`, the commit thread is also stopped before the pool shuts down. Offsets for items that finished in the final window are never committed, so they are reprocessed after reassignment.

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and does no draining either. On rebalance this produces both skipped items (in-memory loss, recovered only by redelivery) and duplicates. Drain the queues, wait for workers, then do a final commit before returning from `join`.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure, despite the docstring

Each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A single slow subscription will therefore let its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, risking OOM. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and raise `MessageRejected` when one is full.

Commits stall permanently when partition offsets are not contiguous

`get_committable_offsets` only advances while every integer offset between `start` and `max_offset` has been seen in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control records, compacted topics, and aborted transactions all leave gaps that the consumer never receives.

Any such gap blocks commits for that partition forever, while `all_offsets` keeps growing. Track contiguity only among the offsets actually received (for example, commit up to just below the lowest outstanding offset), not across absolute integer ranges.

Failed items are committed, contradicting "only commits after successful processing"

The worker's `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raises. Decode and submit failures are also completed immediately. Offsets are therefore committed regardless of processing outcome, which is at-most-once delivery. The class docstring says "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and "No item is lost", which is misleading for anyone relying on it.

Error-handling test asserts no commit, contrary to implementation, and passes only by timing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts that the partition is not committed after one processing failure. The implementation does mark failed offsets complete, so both 100 and 101 become committable and are committed on the next one-second commit tick.

The test passes only because it exits roughly 0.2s after processing finishes, before the commit thread wakes up. It is flaky on slow CI, and it documents behavior the code doesn't have. Assert the real semantics deterministically instead.

The 'advanced' branch passes `cursor.offset < 0` straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySets reject negative indexing with `ValueError`/`AssertionError`, so any client-supplied cursor like `0:-5:0` crashes the request with a 500.

false_positives.candidate:
Switching span buffer keys from SET to ZSET breaks in-flight data on deploy

Existing `span-buf:s:*` keys in Redis are SETs written by the old code. After deploy, several operations hit those keys:
- `zadd` here
- `zcard`/`zunionstore` in `add-buffer.lua`
- `zscan` in `_load_segment_data`

All of these fail with WRONGTYPE errors against SET keys. The consumer and flusher will crash or loop until those keys expire, which can take up to `redis_ttl`, i.e. one hour.

A migration path is needed: new key prefix, a type check, or draining before rollout.

Silent hardcoded eviction replaces configurable span-count limit

The script hardcodes a limit of 1000 and silently `zpopmin`s the excess spans, with no metric and no log.

Meanwhile `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is now unused, and the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and log were removed. The configuration is dead and inconsistent with the actual limit, and data loss is unobservable.

A related problem: `zunionstore` uses the default SUM aggregation, so a payload present in both sets gets a doubled score. That distorts which spans are evicted. The limit should be passed as an ARGV and the eviction counted in a metric.

Redirect depth limit reduced 10x without justification

The redirect-following loop limit was lowered from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining its consequence was removed. Segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now be split into separate segments instead of joined correctly.

No tests for eviction or the new paginator

The PR's headline behavior has no tests:
- trimming segments over 1000 spans via `zpopmin`, and which spans survive
- `OptimizedCursorPaginator`
- the new audit-log branch

A basic test of the paginator would have revealed its datetime and negative-offset crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision ignores the dataset and query actually being executed

`_get_event_stats` passes the outer `dataset` and the raw `request` into `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. It does not use the `scoped_dataset` and `query` arguments it actually runs. In the dashboard split paths, the dataset is switched to `discover` and the query is rewritten, e.g. `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction` or `AND event.type:transaction`. The upsampling decision is still made from the original request, so it can be wrong in both directions:
- errors-only split queries are never upsampled when the outer dataset is metrics-enhanced;
- a transactions-only split query can be upsampled if the user's query text contained `event.type:error`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: passing the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset` into the upsampling check, causing dashboard split queries (where the outer dataset is metrics and the scoped dataset is discover) to skip upsampling.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule (gitlink) committed

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink pointing at the base commit (a5d29095…). It is unrelated to the feature and looks like a local checkout of the repo that got staged by mistake. Merging it adds a broken or recursive submodule entry to the repository, with no `.gitmodules` entry to back it. Remove it from the PR.

Substring check treats negated or other error-type filters as error-focused

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever `"event.type:error"` appears anywhere in the lowercased query string. A query like `!event.type:error` (which excludes errors) contains that substring, so it is treated as error-focused. So is `event.type:errors_foo`. For allowlisted projects on the discover dataset, `count()` is then rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` for non-error events, which have no sample_weight. The result is wrong counts, usually 0. Parse the query, or at least reject negated filters.

Eligibility cache is never invalidated and contradicts its own documentation

Eligibility is cached for 60s per org and project set. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called, even though its docstring says it should run when the allowlist changes. As a result, allowlist changes take up to 60s to apply, and different hosts can return different counts for the same query in that window. The docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` also claims the configuration is read fresh each time, which the cache makes false. Either wire up invalidation or drop the cache.

Cache adds a remote round-trip in front of an already-cached option lookup

The code claims `options.get` is an expensive lookup. In practice options are cached in-process, so `options.get` is cheap. Putting `cache.get` / `cache.set` in front of it adds a memcached or redis round-trip to every `_get_event_stats` call, which makes the request slower rather than faster. The key is also built from Python `hash()` of the project tuple, so two different project sets can collide and share an eligibility result.

upsampled_count silently drops events without sample_weight

`upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no fallback. Events that have no sample_weight contribute nothing to the sum. That includes events ingested before a project was allowlisted, or events whose SDK sent no client sample rate. Once a project is allowlisted, historical or unsampled error counts drop toward 0 instead of counting as 1 each. Use something like `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`. The result type is also declared `number` while `count()` is `integer`, which changes the response meta for the same yAxis.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every new denied resource now bypasses the permission cache and queries the DB

When cached permissions exist but do not grant access, `Check` falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`. That function no longer consults `permCache`, so it always runs the basic-role, team and permission queries against the DB.

The denial cache only short-circuits repeats of the exact (user, action, name, folder) tuple. A user checked against many distinct resources they cannot access triggers a full permission query per resource, for example when filtering a search result set dashboard by dashboard. Singleflight only dedups concurrent identical calls.

Before this change those checks were served from `permCache`. This can multiply DB load substantially for users with restricted access.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying code behavior: when cached permissions exist in `permCache` and grant access, `Check` trusts the cache, whereas when cached permissions do not grant access (a denial), `Check` bypasses/ignores `permCache` and queries the database via `getIdentityPermissions`. While the golden comment frames the inconsistency as a security risk (trusting stale grants while distrusting stale denials) and the candidate frames it as a performance problem (distrusting cached denials causes excessive DB queries), they are pointing to the exact same design flaw and code mechanic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not prove the cache short-circuits

The test claims to "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but it seeds `permCache` with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. A false value is not a grant in `checkPermission`.

The default fake store also returns no permissions. So the request would be denied even if the denial cache were ignored, and the test passes regardless of whether `permDenialCache` works.

The cached value should be `true`, and ideally the test should assert the store was not called.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug in the test: the comment says it allows access to the dashboard, but the cached permissions map sets 'dashboards:uid:dash1' to false instead of true, causing checkPermission to deny access rather than grant it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous denial cache key can deny unrelated resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent with `_` and no escaping. Resource names and folder UIDs may legitimately contain underscores.

For example, (name="a_b", parent="") and (name="a", parent="b") produce the same key. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies access to the other.

The key also shares the `.perm_` prefix with `userPermCacheKey` in the same cache backend, which increases collision risk with differently typed entries. Use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous separator or encoding.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys using unescaped underscore separators, leading to key collisions when components contain underscores or are empty, which can cause incorrect denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Requery does not refresh the stale folder tree, so newly created folders still deny and the denial gets cached

The DB fallback only refreshes the permission scope map. `checkInheritedPermissions` still uses `buildFolderTree`, which is served from `folderCache` (30s TTL).

Scenario: a dashboard sits in a newly created folder whose ancestor grants access. The new folder is missing from the cached tree, so `Ancestors(req.ParentFolder)` yields nothing and the check is denied. That denial is then written to `permDenialCache`, extending the wrong answer.

This is part of the scenario the PR claims to fix (newly created folders) and it remains broken. On a miss, the folder tree should also be refreshed, or the denial should not be cached when the parent folder is absent from the tree.

Denial cache pins stale denials for 30s, undermining the 'requery on miss' fix

Any denial is cached for `shortCacheTTL` (30s), and the denial cache is checked before anything else.

If a check for a resource happens before its permissions are written, the denial sticks. This can occur during a create flow or right before a share or grant. Every subsequent check for that resource then returns denied for 30s without consulting the DB, even after the permission exists.

This reintroduces the delay the PR is trying to eliminate for newly created dashboards and folders. Nothing invalidates the entry when permissions are granted.

false_positives.candidate:
Update skips login-cache invalidation when the org-aware wrapper reports the IDP disabled

`update()` passes `idpById` to `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. `idpById` comes from `getById()`, so it is wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`, and its `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The JPA `getForLogin` query does not look at organization state, so the cached login list can still contain this IDP's id.

Scenario:
1. The organization is disabled.
2. An admin sets `hideOnLogin=true` (or `linkOnly=true`) on one of its IDPs.
3. The original model fails the login predicate because the wrapper says disabled, and the updated model fails it because it is hidden. Both are false, so the method returns early and nothing is invalidated.

The slot should be accepted if any override range for that day contains it.

The slot is rejected only when `slotStartTime` is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override ends but runs past it (e.g. a 60-minute slot at 10:30 with an override ending at 11:00) passes the check. The recurring branch now runs inside the per-reference loop, so the full deletion pass over all of the organizer's calendar credentials repeats once per calendar reference. Each pass uses only the organizer's credentials and only the first `_calendar` reference of each booking. Other collective hosts' recurring events are never deleted, while the organizer's events receive redundant delete calls.

`CalendarEvent` is spread directly into webhook payloads, so `destinationCalendar` changes from an object (or null) to an array, or `[]`. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

The callback was changed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })`. Any error from `getCalendar` (for example a CalendarService constructor throwing on a bad credential key) is now a rejected promise. The enclosing `try/catch` never sees it, so it becomes an unhandled rejection.

Before this change `getCalendar` was synchronous, so a throw was caught and logged. The deletions are also fire-and-forget, so the function returns before they complete.

Each entry is written as `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`. The PR's goal (only loading an app when it is used) is not achieved. Meanwhile every consumer had to become async, which adds the problems listed in the other findings.

There is a second risk: if any single app module fails to import, its promise rejects at load time with no handler attached. That produces an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process depending on configuration.

Async forEach callback escapes the surrounding try/catch

The `forEach(async ...)` callback awaits `getCalendar`, so a failure while loading or constructing the calendar becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The surrounding try/catch cannot catch it, although it could catch the previously synchronous throw.

requestReschedule fires un-awaited async callbacks; getCalendar failures become unhandled rejections

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` is not awaited. If `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` rejects, nothing handles the rejection, and it can crash or log noise in the API process.

The mutation also returns before the old calendar and video events are deleted. Previously a synchronous `getCalendar` throw would have surfaced as a proper TRPC error.

`getCalendarCredentials` still calls `getCalendar(credential)` without awaiting it. The `calendar` field of each returned item is therefore now `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`.

Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`. Any other caller that uses `item.calendar` directly will now operate on a Promise. That includes truthiness checks like `if (!calendar)`, which are always truthy for a Promise, and calls like `calendar.listCalendars()`.

Also, a rejection of a promise created here before `getConnectedCalendars` attaches a handler can surface as an unhandled rejection.

In the recurring branch, `forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(...) })` pushes into `apiDeletes` only after an await. By that point `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 has already captured the array.

As a result, these calendar deletions are never awaited, and any errors they throw are unhandled rejections. The new `await getCalendar` makes this race certain rather than incidental.

- For file-based indexes, `bleve.New` on the same directory fails because the path already exists.
