false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on rebalance, so later messages are silently dropped and committed

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `__init__`, but every `create_with_partitions` call wraps that same pool in a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On a partition revocation or rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy. That calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down every queue and stops every worker permanently.

The next strategy built after reassignment reuses the dead pool:
- `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
- `submit` catches it in its generic `except`, then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for that message.
- The commit loop commits those offsets.

After the first rebalance, every uptime result is dropped but its offset is still committed. Either build the pool per strategy, or don't shut down the shared pool in the strategy's `close()`.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `Commit`, roughly once per second. Arroyo's commit callback is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the strategy's `submit`/`poll` on the consumer thread.

Calling it concurrently with the `StreamProcessor` run loop can corrupt its staged-offset state. It can also commit after the processor has started revoking partitions or shutting down, because `terminate()` doesn't join this thread. Collect committable offsets here, but perform the commit inside `poll()` on the main thread.

Shutdown discards queued work and never commits work that finished after the last tick

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. Each worker exits after its current item, so items still waiting in the queues are never processed. `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)` would normally drain them, but the flag defeats that.

In `close()`, the commit thread is also stopped before the pool shuts down. Offsets for items that finished in the final window are never committed, so they are reprocessed after reassignment.

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and does no draining either. On rebalance this produces both skipped items (in-memory loss, recovered only by redelivery) and duplicates. Drain the queues, wait for workers, then do a final commit before returning from `join`.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure, despite the docstring

Each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A single slow subscription will therefore let its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, risking OOM. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and raise `MessageRejected` when one is full.

Commits stall permanently when partition offsets are not contiguous

`get_committable_offsets` only advances while every integer offset between `start` and `max_offset` has been seen in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control records, compacted topics, and aborted transactions all leave gaps that the consumer never receives.

Any such gap blocks commits for that partition forever, while `all_offsets` keeps growing. Track contiguity only among the offsets actually received (for example, commit up to just below the lowest outstanding offset), not across absolute integer ranges.

Failed items are committed, contradicting "only commits after successful processing"

The worker's `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raises. Decode and submit failures are also completed immediately. Offsets are therefore committed regardless of processing outcome, which is at-most-once delivery. The class docstring says "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and "No item is lost", which is misleading for anyone relying on it.

Error-handling test asserts no commit, contrary to implementation, and passes only by timing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts that the partition is not committed after one processing failure. The implementation does mark failed offsets complete, so both 100 and 101 become committable and are committed on the next one-second commit tick.

The test passes only because it exits roughly 0.2s after processing finishes, before the commit thread wakes up. It is flaky on slow CI, and it documents behavior the code doesn't have. Assert the real semantics deterministically instead.

`workingHours.find` returns true as soon as any working-hour entry for that weekday does not contain the slot, and that makes the slot unavailable. If a host has several ranges on the same day (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17, or ranges split at the UTC day boundary), a slot inside 9-12 lies outside 13-17 and gets rejected. The fix is to reject only when the slot falls outside all applicable ranges (use `some`/`every` correctly). As written, fixed and round-robin hosts with multiple ranges lose valid slots.

`dateOverrides.find` returns true, meaning 'not available', for the first same-day override whose range does not contain the slot. If a user has two override ranges on the same day (e.g. 9-10 and 14-16), a slot at 14:00 is rejected because it falls outside 9-10, even though it fits the second range. The slot should be accepted if any override range for that day contains it.

Override end boundary compares slot start instead of slot end

The slot is rejected only when `slotStartTime` is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override ends but runs past it (e.g. a 60-minute slot at 10:30 with an override ending at 11:00) passes the check. The fixed host is then booked outside their overridden availability. The check should compare `slotEndTime` against the override end.

The override start is shifted by the negated organizer offset and formatted as a date. That date is then compared with the slot's UTC calendar date (`slotStartTime` is `.utc()`). For organizers far from UTC, the organizer's local override day and the slot's UTC day differ near midnight. As a result, overrides can be ignored for slots on the override day, or applied to slots on an adjacent day.

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` parses the locale-style `Date.prototype.toString()` string, which is not ISO 8601. That depends on engine-specific `Date` parsing and drops milliseconds. `override.start` is already a `Date` and should be passed directly.

The PR's main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides restrict round-robin availability, but no test creates a round-robin event with a fixed host that has an override. The mutation also returns before the old calendar and video events are deleted. Previously a synchronous `getCalendar` throw would have surfaced as a proper TRPC error.

That includes truthiness checks like `if (!calendar)`, which are always truthy for a Promise, and calls like `calendar.listCalendars()`.

Also, a rejection of a promise created here before `getConnectedCalendars` attaches a handler can surface as an unhandled rejection.

In the recurring branch, `forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(...) })` pushes into `apiDeletes` only after an await. By that point `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 has already captured the array.

As a result, these calendar deletions are never awaited, and any errors they throw are unhandled rejections. The new `await getCalendar` makes this race certain rather than incidental.

Now the lock is taken only to store the result. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does a check-then-build (`GetIndex` returns nil, then `build`), so two callers can build the same `NamespacedResource` concurrently. Typical callers are two `Search` requests, or a `Search` request racing the async `handleEvent` watcher. The consequences are:
- Duplicate full ListIterator scans.
- The second cache store silently replaces the first index, so writes made to the losing instance are lost.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted.
- For file-based indexes, `bleve.New` on the same directory fails because the path already exists.

The code needs per-key build deduplication, e.g. singleflight or a per-key mutex, rather than either one global lock or none.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on rebalance, so later messages are silently dropped and committed

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `__init__`, but every `create_with_partitions` call wraps that same pool in a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On a partition revocation or rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy. That calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down every queue and stops every worker permanently.

The next strategy built after reassignment reuses the dead pool:
- `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
- `submit` catches it in its generic `except`, then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for that message.
- The commit loop commits those offsets.

After the first rebalance, every uptime result is dropped but its offset is still committed. Either build the pool per strategy, or don't shut down the shared pool in the strategy's `close()`.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `Commit`, roughly once per second. Arroyo's commit callback is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the strategy's `submit`/`poll` on the consumer thread.

Calling it concurrently with the `StreamProcessor` run loop can corrupt its staged-offset state. It can also commit after the processor has started revoking partitions or shutting down, because `terminate()` doesn't join this thread. Collect committable offsets here, but perform the commit inside `poll()` on the main thread.

Shutdown discards queued work and never commits work that finished after the last tick

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. Each worker exits after its current item, so items still waiting in the queues are never processed. `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)` would normally drain them, but the flag defeats that.

In `close()`, the commit thread is also stopped before the pool shuts down. Offsets for items that finished in the final window are never committed, so they are reprocessed after reassignment.

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and does no draining either. On rebalance this produces both skipped items (in-memory loss, recovered only by redelivery) and duplicates. Drain the queues, wait for workers, then do a final commit before returning from `join`.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure, despite the docstring

Each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A single slow subscription will therefore let its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, risking OOM. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and raise `MessageRejected` when one is full.

Commits stall permanently when partition offsets are not contiguous

`get_committable_offsets` only advances while every integer offset between `start` and `max_offset` has been seen in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control records, compacted topics, and aborted transactions all leave gaps that the consumer never receives.

Any such gap blocks commits for that partition forever, while `all_offsets` keeps growing. Track contiguity only among the offsets actually received (for example, commit up to just below the lowest outstanding offset), not across absolute integer ranges.

Failed items are committed, contradicting "only commits after successful processing"

The worker's `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raises. Decode and submit failures are also completed immediately. Offsets are therefore committed regardless of processing outcome, which is at-most-once delivery. The class docstring says "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and "No item is lost", which is misleading for anyone relying on it.

Error-handling test asserts no commit, contrary to implementation, and passes only by timing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts that the partition is not committed after one processing failure. The implementation does mark failed offsets complete, so both 100 and 101 become committable and are committed on the next one-second commit tick.

The test passes only because it exits roughly 0.2s after processing finishes, before the commit thread wakes up. It is flaky on slow CI, and it documents behavior the code doesn't have. Assert the real semantics deterministically instead.

However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes redundant manifest reloads

The fast path reads `entryPointAssetsCache` under RLock and releases it. It then takes the write lock and unconditionally reloads, without checking the cache again.

At startup or after a cache miss, many concurrent requests can all see `nil`. Each one then queues on the write lock and re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` in turn, even though the first goroutine already populated the cache. If the CDN path is enabled, each would also issue an HTTP request.

Add a second check after `Lock()` (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`), or use `sync.Once`/singleflight for the non-dev case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing second cache check after acquiring the write lock, which allows concurrent goroutines to redundantly reload the manifest.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

If an operator sets `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` above that limit, every cleanup batch fails, whereas the previous subquery-based statement had no parameter limit. Quadratic string building for inlined SQLite IDs

The loop at lines 610-612 runs `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` once per ID. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n²) in the number of IDs. With the large batch sizes this branch exists for (e.g. 32767, as in the new test), that means heavy allocation and CPU work on every batch. Use a `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` into a single byte buffer instead.

The legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection calls will therefore often fail with `context canceled` before they finish, so legacy storage silently drifts out of sync. The same pattern is at lines 110, 135 and 163. The parent should be `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` so logger values are kept but cancellation is not.

Legacy write failures in background goroutines are never logged

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage errors are therefore reported as legacy errors, and storage error metrics are missing. Update has the same mistake at line 129.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.

Unbounded, unvalidated limit/offset on public members endpoint

`limit` and `offset` are taken straight from user params, with no cap and no lower bound. This endpoint is reachable by any user who can see the group, not just admins.

- A request with `limit=10000000` serializes every member of a huge automatic group such as trust_level_0. That is an easy way to load the database and app server.
- A negative `limit` or `offset` is passed to Postgres. Postgres rejects negative LIMIT/OFFSET, so the request fails with a 500.

Clamp `limit` to a sane maximum (e.g. 1..200) and clamp `offset` to >= 0.

Breaking change to /groups/:id/members response shape

The endpoint used to return a bare JSON array of users. It now returns `{members: [...], meta: {...}}`, and non-automatic groups are now paginated to 50 by default where previously the full list was returned.

Any other client of this endpoint will silently break or receive truncated data. That includes external API consumers, plugins, and other front-end code that calls `/groups/:name/members` and expects an array.

The change and default limit should be documented, or existing consumers audited.

Admin create/update no longer accept nested `group[...]` params or usernames

API clients that still send nested `group` params will create groups with an empty name, which fails validation. On update they will silently reset `visible` to false, because `params[:visible]` is nil.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.

The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:

`cook` returns `raw` verbatim for `raw_html` posts. Content pulled from RSS feeds or remote pages via Readability is then stored and served as trusted HTML; Readability is not a security sanitizer.

Any script, iframe or event-handler attributes in the source page or feed are rendered on the forum. The same applies to anyone who later edits such a post, since `cook_method` persists. Run the HTML through a sanitizer (e.g. Sanitize with a whitelist) before storing or rendering it.

Failed post creation still creates TopicEmbed with nil ids

`PostCreator#create` returns the unsaved `@post` even when it rolled back (spam detection, topic creation errors such as a duplicate title). `post.present?` is true for that object, so `TopicEmbed.create!` runs with `post_id`/`topic_id` nil.

The columns are NOT NULL, so this raises a DB error and the job or import crashes. Check `post.persisted?` / `creator.errors` instead.

Protocol-relative URLs are mangled by absolutize_urls

`href`/`src` values starting with `//` (protocol-relative, e.g. `//cdn.example.com/img.png`) pass the `start_with?('/')` check. After the leading slashes are stripped they become `http://embedhost/cdn.example.com/img.png`, which breaks every protocol-relative link and image in imported content.

If the process dies between `setnx` and `expire`, the key never expires. Retrieval for that URL is then throttled forever. Use `SET key 1 NX EX 60` atomically.

The `--category` option was removed, and the topic's original `created_at` is no longer applied, which is a behavior regression for existing users of the task.
